newsitem.title: UK: Britain urges Beijing rethink Hong Kong policy.
newsitem.headline: Britain urges Beijing rethink Hong Kong policy.

text.p: Britain on Friday urged China to reconsider its plans to set up a provisional legislature for Hong Kong and said there was no justification for the move.

In a toughly worded statement, Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind called on the international community to maintain pressure on Beijing in the run-up to the colony being handed back to China on June 30 next year.

The legislature is to be formed this Saturday by a China-controlled, 400-member Selection Committee that is meeting over the border in the city of Shenzhen in case of any legal challenge in the Hong Kong courts.
Britain has constantly attacked the move as one not envisioned in handover agreements and questioned its legality.
Rifkind, defending Hong Kong's current legislative council, said: "There is no justification for China to replace a legislature elected openly and fairly by more than one million Hong Kong people."
"China should be prepared to trust Hong Kong people with the measure of democracy we have introduced," he said in a statement.

Rifkind was even blunter in an interview with The Financial Times, telling the paper: "The very creation of a provisional legislature is a very foolish step. It is one we hope they will reflect further on before anything irreversible is done."
"It is an extremely unwise initiative on their part. We are very unhappy," he said.
He summoned Jiang Enzhu, China's Ambassador to Britain, on Thursday night to underline Britain's concern.
Rifkind pledged that the British government will step up its monitoring of Hong Kong developments both before and after the handover.
The government will report to parliament every six months with particular attention paid to protecting human rights in Hong Kong, he said.

In his statement, Rifkind said: "We will work closely with the United States, the European Union and other international partners in monitoring observance of provisions of the joint declaration in Hong Kong after the handover."
He said Britain had been in touch with governments around the world in the last week to ensure they keep up the pressure on Beijing.
China, upset by electoral reforms in the last years of British rule, has sworn to install the interim body to replace the elected legislature after the 1997 handover.
Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa has attacked the British and Hong Kong governments for refusing to recognise it.

The former shipping company boss said the controversy over the assembly could be swiftly resolved by China's parliament passing a law to make its legality rock-solid if people continued to question its legitimacy.
